title: Mixed Precision and Quantization Theory
summary: This day covers essential concepts for building AI engineering skills.
content:
# Mixed Precision and Quantization Theory ##### The gradient that became zero A team in Chennai was training a 1.3B model in fp16. Loss descended normally for 4,000 steps, then flattened. Not diverged — flattened. Gradient norm read 0.0000 for entire stretches. Their `GradScaler` was doing its job on the large gradients. The problem was the small ones. In fp16, the smallest normal positive number is about 6.1e-5, and subnormals bottom out around 6e-8. A gradient of 3e-9 — perfectly ordinary in a deep network's early layers — rounds to exactly zero. Those layers had stopped receiving any signal at all. The model was still training, but only its top third. Switching to bf16 fixed it in one line. bf16's smallest normal is about 1.2e-38, so 3e-9 is comfortably representable. **The two formats have the same 16 bits and allocate them completely differently**, and that allocation decides whether your training works. Today is about numeric formats — for training and for the quantization that makes serving affordable. ##### How floating point allocates bits A float is sign, exponent, and mantissa. The exponent sets **range**; the mantissa sets **precision**. ``` FP32 [S][EEEEEEEE][MMMMMMMMMMMMMMMMMMMMMMM] 1+8+23 FP16 [S][EEEEE][MMMMMMMMMM] 1+5+10 BF16 [S][EEEEEEEE][MMMMMMM] 1+8+7 FP8 E4M3 [S][EEEE][MMM] 1+4+3 FP8 E5M2 [S][EEEEE][MM] 1+5+2 ``` | Format | Bits | Exp | Mantissa | Max | Min normal | Decimal digits | |---|---|---|---|---|---|---| | FP32 | 32 | 8 | 23 | 3.4e38 | 1.2e-38 | ~7 | | FP16 | 16 | 5 | 10 | 65,504 | 6.1e-5 | ~3 | | **BF16** | 16 | **8** | 7 | **3.4e38** | **1.2e-38** | ~2 | | FP8 E4M3 | 8 | 4 | 3 | 448 | 2^-6 | ~1 | | FP8 E5M2 | 8 | 5 | 2 | 57,344 | 2^-14 | ~1 | **BF16 is FP32 with the mantissa truncated.** Same exponent width, same range — you lose precision, not dynamic range. That single design choice is why it works for deep learning. ```python import torch x = torch.tensor([3e-9, 1e-8, 6e-5, 1.0, 65504.0, 1e6]) print("fp32:", x) print("fp16:", x.half()) # tensor([0., 1.0014e-08, 6.0022e-05, 1., 65504., inf], dtype=torch.float16) print("bf16:", x.bfloat16()) # tensor([3.0035e-09, 1.0012e-08, 5.9843e-05, 1., 65536., 1.0000e+06]) ``` Read the fp16 row carefully. `3e-9` became **zero** — that is the Chennai bug. And `1e6` became **inf** — the overflow half of the same problem. ##### Why BF16 wins for LLMs Three reasons, in order of importance. **1. Gradients span an enormous dynamic range.** In a deep network, gradient magnitudes routinely range from 1e-10 to 1e2 across layers. fp16 covers about five orders of magnitude before underflowing; bf16 covers thirty-eight. **2. No loss scaling needed.** fp16 training requires a `GradScaler` that multiplies the loss by a large factor before backward, then divides the gradients after, dynamically adjusting the factor when it detects overflow. It works, mostly, and adds a failure mode. bf16 needs none of it. **3. Simple conversion.** bf16 is literally fp32 with the low 16 mantissa bits dropped. Conversion is a truncation, and casting back is exact for values that started as bf16. ```python import torch def fp16_training_step(model, x, y, optimizer, scaler): """fp16 requires a GradScaler and can still silently underflow.""" with torch.autocast("cuda", dtype=torch.float16): loss = criterion(model(x), y) scaler.scale(loss).backward() scaler.unscale_(optimizer) # for gradient clipping torch.nn.utils.clip_grad_norm_(model.parameters(), 1.0) scaler.step(optimizer) scaler.update() # adjusts the scale factor optimizer.zero_grad(set_to_none=True) def bf16_training_step(model, x, y, optimizer): """bf16 needs no scaler.""" with torch.autocast("cuda", dtype=torch.bfloat16): loss = criterion(model(x), y) loss.backward() torch.nn.utils.clip_grad_norm_(model.parameters(), 1.0) optimizer.step() optimizer.zero_grad(set_to_none=True) ``` **The precision cost is real but tolerable.** bf16 has about 2–3 decimal digits against fp16's 3–4. It matters for accumulation, which is why mixed precision keeps certain things in fp32. **Use bf16 on Ampere or newer (A100, H100, RTX 30/40 series).** On older hardware — V100, T4 — bf16 is unsupported and fp16 with a scaler is your only option. ##### What mixed precision actually keeps in fp32 "Mixed" is the operative word. The pattern: ```mermaid flowchart TD A["FP32 master weights"] --> B["Cast to BF16"] B --> C["Forward pass in BF16
matmuls on tensor cores"] C --> D["Loss computed in FP32"] D --> E["Backward in BF16"] E --> F["Gradients cast to FP32"] F --> G["Optimizer update in FP32
Adam m, v in FP32"] G --> A H["Kept in FP32:
softmax, LayerNorm,
loss reduction,
optimizer state"] -.-> D ``` **Reductions stay in fp32.** Summing 4,096 bf16 values accumulates rounding error badly; PyTorch's autocast keeps softmax, layer norm, and loss reduction in fp32 automatically. **Master weights stay in fp32.** With bf16 weights, an update of 1e-8 against a weight of 1.0 is entirely lost to rounding — the weight simply never changes. Keeping an fp32 copy preserves those small updates and applies them cumulatively. ```python # Demonstrating why master weights matter w_bf16 = torch.tensor([1.0], dtype=torch.bfloat16) w_fp32 = torch.tensor([1.0], dtype=torch.float32) update = 1e-4 for _ in range(1000): w_bf16 = (w_bf16 + update).bfloat16() w_fp32 = w_fp32 + update print(f"bf16 after 1000 updates: {w_bf16.item():.6f}") # 1.000000 — nothing happened print(f"fp32 after 1000 updates: {w_fp32.item():.6f}") # 1.100000 — correct ``` That is the whole argument for the extra 4 bytes per parameter in the memory budget from Day 1. ##### FP8 H100 and newer support fp8 in hardware, roughly doubling throughput again. Two variants exist because forward and backward have different needs: **E4M3** (more mantissa, less range) for weights and activations, **E5M2** (more range, less mantissa) for gradients, which span wider magnitudes. FP8 requires **per-tensor scaling factors** tracked with a delayed-scaling scheme — you record the max absolute value over recent steps and scale accordingly. NVIDIA's Transformer Engine handles this: ```python import transformer_engine.pytorch as te from transformer_engine.common.recipe import Format, DelayedScaling fp8_recipe = DelayedScaling( fp8_format=Format.HYBRID, # E4M3 forward, E5M2 backward amax_history_len=16, amax_compute_algo="max", ) with te.fp8_autocast(enabled=True, fp8_recipe=fp8_recipe): out = te_model(x) ``` Reported results are roughly 1.6–2× the throughput of bf16 with negligible quality loss on large models. It is not yet the default because it needs H100-class hardware and careful scaling, but it is the direction. ##### Quantization: the inference problem Training precision is about gradient fidelity. Inference precision is about **memory bandwidth**, which Day 2 established as the binding constraint during decoding. A 7B model in bf16 is 14 GB. Every generated token reads all 14 GB from HBM. At INT4 it is 3.5 GB — a 4× reduction in the thing that actually limits you. **Uniform affine quantization** maps floats to integers: $$q = \text{round}\left(\frac{x}{s}\right) + z, \qquad x \approx s \cdot (q - z)$$ where `s` is the scale and `z` the zero point. ```python import torch def quantize_tensor(x, n_bits=8, symmetric=True, per_channel_dim=None): """Uniform affine quantization with optional per-channel scales.""" qmin = -(2 ** (n_bits - 1)) if symmetric else 0 qmax = 2 ** (n_bits - 1) - 1 if symmetric else 2 ** n_bits - 1 if per_channel_dim is not None: dims = [d for d in range(x.ndim) if d != per_channel_dim] amax = x.abs().amax(dim=dims, keepdim=True) xmin = x.amin(dim=dims, keepdim=True) xmax = x.amax(dim=dims, keepdim=True) else: amax, xmin, xmax = x.abs().max(), x.min(), x.max() if symmetric: scale = amax / qmax zero = torch.zeros_like(scale) else: scale = (xmax - xmin) / (qmax - qmin) zero = qmin - torch.round(xmin / scale) q = torch.clamp(torch.round(x / scale) + zero, qmin, qmax) return q, scale, zero def dequantize(q, scale, zero): return scale * (q - zero) w = torch.randn(512, 512) for bits in [8, 4]: for per_ch in [None, 0]: q, s, z = quantize_tensor(w, bits, per_channel_dim=per_ch) err = (dequantize(q, s, z) - w).abs().mean().item() label = "per-channel" if per_ch is not None else "per-tensor " print(f"INT{bits} {label}: mean abs error {err:.5f}") ``` **Per-channel scaling is substantially better than per-tensor**, because different output channels of a weight matrix have very different magnitude ranges. One shared scale is dominated by the largest channel and crushes the rest. **Group-wise quantization** goes further — a separate scale per group of 64 or 128 weights. This is what makes INT4 viable, and it is what NF4 (from Day 29's QLoRA) uses. ##### PTQ versus QAT **Post-training quantization** takes a trained model and quantizes it. No retraining, minutes to run. ```python def ptq_calibrate(model, calibration_loader, n_batches=32): """Collect activation ranges to set quantization scales.""" ranges = {} def make_hook(name): def hook(mod, inp, out): t = out.detach() lo, hi = t.min().item(), t.max().item() if name in ranges: ranges[name] = (min(ranges[name][0], lo), max(ranges[name][1], hi)) else: ranges[name] = (lo, hi) return hook handles = [m.register_forward_hook(make_hook(n)) for n, m in model.named_modules() if isinstance(m, torch.nn.Linear)] model.eval() with torch.no_grad(): for i, batch in enumerate(calibration_loader): if i >= n_batches: break model(batch) for h in handles: h.remove() return ranges ``` **Calibration data matters more than people expect.** 128–512 samples from your actual distribution is the standard, and using out-of-domain calibration data measurably hurts. For a Hindi-language deployment, calibrate on Hindi. **Quantization-aware training** simulates quantization during training using a straight-through estimator, so the model learns weights robust to it: ```python class FakeQuantize(torch.autograd.Function): @staticmethod def forward(ctx, x, scale, qmin, qmax): q = torch.clamp(torch.round(x / scale), qmin, qmax) return q * scale @staticmethod def backward(ctx, grad_out): return grad_out, None, None, None # straight-through ``` | | PTQ | QAT | |---|---|---| | Retraining | None | Full or partial | | Time | Minutes | Hours to days | | INT8 quality | Excellent | Excellent | | INT4 quality | Good with GPTQ/AWQ | Better | | Below INT4 | Poor | Viable | **Use PTQ.** For LLMs at INT8 and INT4, modern PTQ methods (GPTQ, AWQ — Day 33) get close enough to QAT that the retraining cost is rarely justified. ##### The outlier problem The reason naive INT8 fails on LLMs, and the finding that motivated most modern methods. Dettmers et al. (LLM.int8, 2022) discovered that transformer activations contain **systematic outliers** — a small number of feature dimensions with magnitudes 20–100× the rest, appearing consistently in the same dimensions across tokens. ```python def find_outliers(activations, threshold=6.0): """Outliers concentrate in specific feature dimensions.""" absact = activations.abs() per_dim_max = absact.amax(dim=tuple(range(activations.ndim - 1))) median = per_dim_max.median() outlier_dims = (per_dim_max > threshold * median).nonzero().flatten() return { "n_outlier_dims": len(outlier_dims), "pct_of_dims": round(100 * len(outlier_dims) / len(per_dim_max), 2), "max_ratio": round((per_dim_max.max() / median).item(), 1), } ``` Typically about 0.1% of dimensions, with 50× the median magnitude — and quantizing them together with everything else destroys precision for the 99.9%. **The three responses:** - **LLM.int8** — keep outlier dimensions in fp16, quantize the rest to INT8. Mixed-precision decomposition. - **SmoothQuant** — migrate difficulty from activations to weights by rescaling, since weights are easier to quantize. - **AWQ** — identify the ~1% of weight channels that matter most (by activation magnitude) and protect them with per-channel scaling. This is why "just cast to int8" does not work for LLMs while it works fine for CNNs. ##### What to quantize | Target | Typical | Benefit | Risk | |---|---|---|---| | **Weights** | INT8, INT4 | Memory, bandwidth | Low with good methods | | **Activations** | INT8 | Compute speed | Outliers | | **KV cache** | INT8, FP8 | Large memory saving at long context | Moderate | | **Gradients** | Rarely | Communication | High | **Weight-only quantization is the default for LLM serving.** Weights are static so you quantize once; activations stay in bf16, avoiding the outlier problem entirely. You get the memory and bandwidth win, which is what matters during decode, without the accuracy risk. **KV cache quantization** is underused and worth knowing about — at long context the cache exceeds the weights (Day 2), and INT8 KV cache typically costs under a point of perplexity. ##### Common mistakes - **fp16 for LLM training** on hardware that supports bf16 — the underflow-to-zero failure. - **No fp32 master weights**, so small updates vanish entirely. - **Reductions in bf16**, accumulating error across long sums. - **Per-tensor quantization** where per-channel or group-wise is nearly free. - **Calibrating on out-of-domain data.** - **Naive INT8 on activations** without handling outliers. - **Assuming quantization always speeds things up.** It reduces memory traffic; if you are compute-bound, gains are small. - **Quantizing embedding and output layers** aggressively — they are sensitive and relatively small. - **Reaching for QAT** when PTQ with GPTQ or AWQ would suffice. - **Not measuring quality after quantization.** Always run your eval suite. - **fp8 without proper scaling recipes**, which diverges. ##### Hands-on: measure all three Your practical task trains the same small model in FP32, FP16, and BF16, comparing memory, speed, and final loss. Use a model deep enough to show the effect — twelve layers minimum — and log gradient norms per layer. In the fp16 run, watch the early layers' gradient norms; if they hit exactly zero, you have reproduced the Chennai bug on purpose, which is the best way to understand it. The mini project quantizes a model to INT8 with PTQ and measures accuracy loss against speedup. Do it three ways — per-tensor, per-channel, and group-wise at group size 128 — and report perplexity plus tokens/second for each. The typical finding is that per-channel costs almost nothing while per-tensor costs several points, which is a useful thing to have measured yourself. The assignment explains why BF16 beats FP16 for LLM training with numeric examples. Use the tensor comparison from earlier in this article, show the accumulated-update experiment demonstrating why fp32 master weights are needed, and explain the `GradScaler` machinery that bf16 makes unnecessary. Concrete numbers — `3e-9` becoming exactly `0.` — are far more convincing than a description of exponent widths. ##### Key takeaways - **BF16 is FP32 with a truncated mantissa** — same range, less precision — which is exactly the right trade for gradients spanning many orders of magnitude. - **FP16 underflows small gradients to zero and overflows large activations to inf**, which is why it needs a `GradScaler` and why bf16 is the default on Ampere and newer. - **Mixed precision keeps reductions, loss, and optimizer state in fp32**, and fp32 master weights are what preserve updates too small to change a bf16 weight. - **Weight-only quantization is the default for serving** because decoding is memory-bandwidth bound; per-channel or group-wise scales are near-free and much better than per-tensor. - **Transformer activations have systematic outliers** in ~0.1% of dimensions at 50× the median, which is why naive INT8 fails on LLMs and why SmoothQuant, LLM.int8, and AWQ exist.
